newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ABB Q1 seen flat, just like 1997.
newsitem.headline: ABB Q1 seen flat, just like 1997.

text.p: Electrical engineering group ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG should report a roughly flat net profit for the first quarter of 1997 on Tuesday, the second year in a row when earnings will be restrained by Europe's sluggish growth.
Operating profit forecasts are less optimistic, partially reflecting a new reporting practice that will lower operating earnings, but increase financial items for a zero net effect.
Expectations for ABB's first quarter are generally low-key with many analysts still smarting from ABB's disappointing 1996 results, which triggered downgradings and forecasts reductions.
Despite red faces, analysts' fundamental belief in ABB and its management is unshaken and hopes are pinned on ABB returning to a phase of strong earnings growth from 1998 to 2000.
"ABB is actually doing fantastically well given the environment," said Andrew Griffen of UBS.
On average 12 analysts in Zurich, Stockholm and London forecast a first quarter net profit of $223 million, or a gain of 1.8 percent from 219 million in the first quarter of 1996.
The forecasts range from $213 million to $240 million.
"Expectations are not high for the first quarter," said Paola Orler of Zurich Kantonalbank.
ABB's operating profit is forecast to drop 10.7 percent to $540 million from last year's $605 million. Forecasts range from $410 million to $625 million.
The first quarter is traditionally ABB's weakest quarter with earnings accounting for 15-20 percent of full-year profits.
The firmer dollar will tend to lower ABB group results, which are reported in dollars.
Analysts will be focusing on any signs that ABB's orders reflect a pickup in Europe and comments about ABB's Power Generation segment, one of the main disappointments in 1996.
Operating earnings in power generation fell 39 percent to $561 million in 1996, sharply below expectations.

Although power generation has become less of a driver of ABB's earnings growth, analysts are eager to see the effects of recent restructuring efforts and whether the sharp drop in 1996 earnings can be reversed.
Analysts are not expecting any stimulus from Europe in the first quarter, but sometime during the second half.
ABB has said Europe is in the second year of a downturn in ABB's business cycle and an upturn is not expected until 1998.
ABB's 1996 results, which showed a 16 percent rise in net profit on a comparable basis, disappointed analysts who cut their forecasts and in many cases downgraded the shares.
"It was the first time there was a major disappointment," said Peter Gachnang of Bank Julius Baer.
On average analysts slashed 1997 net profit forecasts by 10 percent and currently estimate that ABB's net profit this year will rise a mere 4.2 percent to $1.285 billion.
Forecasts for 1998 were also cut by eight percent after the results and now look for a net profit of $1.571 billion.

Beginning with the first quarter report, ABB will no longer be reporting interest on customer advances, an item that tended to inflate operating earnings. Most other companies do not specify interest earned on advance payments on major projects.
In the past utilities typically paid 15 to 20 percent up front when they ordered a power plant.
ABB booked this payment as revenue, but deducted the imputed interest earned on the downpayment in its financial items.
However, interest on advances has been declining in recent years, part of the reason that operating earnings at ABB's Power Generation segment has been falling.
In 1996 interest on advances fell 18 percent to $807 million and Power Generation accounts for roughly half of the interest.
Competition is fierce in the power area and this affects not only prices, but also financing methods.
Utilities are gradually being replaced by Independent Power Producers (IPPs) -- who act more like bankers than engineers -- and advance payments are becoming more difficult to arrange.
The interest and advance payment was used as working capital so the negative consequence is that ABB now has to finance the projects from its own working capital, a spokesman said.
